previous_disclosures.section: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > 2023 compared with 2022
previous_disclosures.summary: Investment banking fees decreased in 2023 compared with 2022, primarily due to lower advisory fees from reduced transaction activity and lower debt underwriting fees, which were partially offset by higher equity underwriting fees.

Investment Banking revenue was $6.2 billion, down 4%; excluding $257 million of markdowns in 2022, it was down 8%, driven by lower advisory and debt underwriting fees, partially offset by higher equity underwriting fees. The firm ranked #1 for Global Investment Banking fees according to Dealogic.

Debt underwriting fees were $2.6 billion, down 8%, as challenging market conditions, primarily in the first half of the year, resulted in lower issuance activity across leveraged loans, investment-grade loans, and high-grade bonds, largely offset by higher issuance activity in high-yield bonds.

Equity underwriting fees were $1.2 billion, up 11%, driven by higher levels of follow-on offerings due to lower equity market volatility and higher convertible securities offerings, partially offset by lower private placement activity.

comparisons.peer_summary: Investment Banking revenues increased 38%, fueled by a 42% rise in fees from rebounding wallet activity and gains across products, including a 61% increase in DCM underwriting fees due to record debt issuance and a 38% increase in equity underwriting fees from stronger follow-on and convertibles activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPMorgan and Citigroup reported substantial growth in investment banking fees in 2024, driven by increased debt underwriting and broader market recovery. JPMorgan cited a 37% increase in fees, with debt underwriting up 55% due to 'higher industry-wide issuances in leveraged loans, and in high-grade and high-yield bonds.' Citigroup reported a 42% increase in investment banking fees, highlighting a 61% increase in DCM (debt capital markets) underwriting fees due to 'near record debt issuance, particularly in investment grade and higher leveraged finance activity.' Both institutions explicitly linked their debt underwriting growth to leveraged finance and investment-grade issuance trends.
